title: Multicollinearity Detector MicroSim
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Raise the correlation between square feet and rooms, read the correlation matrix and each feature's variance inflation factor, and watch the coefficient confidence intervals widen while R-squared barely moves.

educational.topic: Multicollinearity and the variance inflation factor
learningObjectives: Students will be able to diagnose multicollinearity from a correlation matrix and variance inflation factors, judge whether individual coefficients can be trusted, and evaluate the trade-off in removing a correlated feature.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Simulation with a correlation slider, repeated sampling, and a remedy the student can switch on and off
keyQuestions: Why does R² stay about the same while the intervals for two of the coefficients become very wide?
Why is the VIF of age near 1 even when the other two VIFs are above 10?
After rooms is removed, why does the square feet coefficient move away from 40?
commonMisconceptions: Multicollinearity makes the model predict badly (predictions and R² are largely unaffected; it is the individual coefficients that become unreliable).
A high VIF means the feature is unimportant (it means the feature's information overlaps with other features, so its separate effect is hard to estimate).
Removing a correlated feature has no cost (the remaining coefficient absorbs part of the removed feature's effect and no longer means the same thing).
Two features are a problem only when their correlation is exactly 1 (coefficients become unstable well before that; a correlation of 0.95 already gives a VIF near 10).
assessmentOpportunities: Shown a correlation matrix and a table of VIFs for a new set of features, students identify the features with a multicollinearity problem, state what a VIF of 9 implies about the standard error of that coefficient (it is 3 times as large), and recommend one remedy together with its cost.
